name: Harbour Frost
geological_features: Sheltered ice harbours where glacier tongues meet a partially frozen sea
Towering ice cliffs calving into dark polar waters
Geothermally heated valleys sustaining liquid water year-round
specific_features: Cold-adapted forests of crystalline-structured organisms in the geothermal valleys
description: Harbour Frost is a medium ice world that has achieved a remarkable equilibrium — cold enough to maintain vast ice sheets and glaciers across most of its surface, but geothermally active enough to sustain pockets of liquid water and a breathable atmosphere of surprising richness. The most dramatic features are the ice harbours, sheltered bays where glacier tongues reach the sea and calve towering icebergs into dark, frigid water. The geothermal valleys cut through the ice like green wounds, their warmth sustaining ecosystems that contrast sharply with the frozen waste surrounding them.

The breathable atmosphere is a product of the geothermal valley ecosystems, whose flora produce oxygen in quantities sufficient to maintain a viable atmospheric composition across the entire planet. The air is thin and bitterly cold outside the valleys, but within them, temperatures hover near zero and the atmosphere thickens noticeably. The transition from ice desert to living valley is abrupt and dramatic — a few hundred meters can separate lifeless frozen plain from a dense forest of crystalline organisms that chime in the wind like glass bells.

The crystalline flora are unlike any known biological system, their structures incorporating mineral frameworks that give them a translucent, jewel-like quality. They grow slowly but persist for centuries, their mineral-organic hybrid biology resistant to the cold that presses in from every side. Biochemical analysis suggests they may represent a parallel evolutionary path where biology incorporated crystallographic principles from the outset, producing organisms that are as much mineral as they are alive.

Harbour Frost's geothermal valleys have been proposed as settlement sites, their relatively mild conditions and breathable air making them among the most hospitable locations on any ice world. A small research community has established itself in the largest valley, studying the crystalline flora and monitoring the geothermal systems that sustain the habitable zones. The ice harbours serve as natural ports for the submersible vehicles that explore the under-ice ocean, adding another layer of accessibility to a world that is cold but far from dead.
